original_question: Explain in what precise sense the volume-preserving diffeomorphism group D_mu(M), equipped with the right-invariant L2 metric, fails to be an infinite-dimensional locally symmetric Riemannian space, and relate that failure to the gap between sectional-curvature intuition and hydrodynamic stability.
target_in_paper: Section 5.3, Problem 11, together with the paragraph immediately before it and the paradox discussion immediately after it: “How ‘far’ is D_μ(M) from being an infinite-dimensional (locally) symmetric Riemannian space?”
correct_elements: The draft correctly identifies the exact geometric object D_μ(M), the right-invariant L2 kinetic-energy metric, the paper’s focus on failure of (local) symmetry, and the motivating mismatch between sectional-curvature heuristics and hydrodynamic stability.
missing_details: The paper’s official formulation is not merely to ‘explain’ the failure, but to ask how far D_μ(M) is from being an infinite-dimensional (locally) symmetric Riemannian space.
The ambient geometric data should be stated: M is an n-dimensional Riemannian manifold and μ is its Riemannian volume form; D_μ(M) is the group of smooth volume-preserving diffeomorphisms of M.
The L2 metric should be identified explicitly as Arnold’s kinetic-energy metric, given at the identity by ⟨v,w⟩_{L2}=∫_M ⟨v(x),w(x)⟩ dμ for divergence-free vector fields v,w.
The precise nearby meaning of the failure of symmetry is that the geodesic central symmetry about the identity in D_μ(M) is not an isometry of the L2 metric.

The paper insists that this geodesic central symmetry must be distinguished from the group-theoretic inversion g↦g^{-1}; the latter is not the relevant symmetry, and on Sobolev completions D^s_μ(M) it is not even differentiable, while on Hölder C^{k,α} models it is not even continuous.
To match the paper’s motivating paradox, the draft should specify the example of the parallel sinusoidal steady flow on the two-torus with stream function ψ=cos(ky).

The curvature statement should be made as in the paper: Arnold’s theorem concerns the group of exact area-preserving torus diffeomorphisms and says that sectional curvature is nonpositive in all, and negative in most, 2-planes containing the direction ψ.

The stability side should be stated in the paper’s concrete terms: some plane-parallel flows are nevertheless Eulerian stable, for example flows with convex velocity profiles on sufficiently short tori.

The paper’s explanation of the gap should be included: the heuristic linking curvature sign to geodesic instability is valid for symmetric spaces, e.g. groups with bi-invariant metrics, but D_μ(M) is instead described as ‘chiral’, i.e. geometrically twisted in one direction.
The draft does not indicate that the paradox is presented as motivation/context for Problem 11, not as a separate broader stability problem.
refined_question: For an n-dimensional Riemannian manifold (M,μ), let D_μ(M) be the group of smooth μ-preserving diffeomorphisms equipped with Arnold’s right-invariant kinetic-energy L2 metric ⟨v,w⟩_{L2}=∫_M ⟨v,w⟩ dμ on divergence-free vector fields. How far is D_μ(M) from being an infinite-dimensional locally symmetric Riemannian space? In particular, make precise that the geodesic central symmetry about the identity is a smooth map but not an L2-isometry, distinguish this from the group inversion g↦g^{-1}, and explain how this non-symmetric (‘chiral’) geometry resolves Arnold’s paradox on T2: for the steady flow with stream function ψ=cos(ky), the sectional curvature of the group of exact area-preserving torus diffeomorphisms is nonpositive in every 2-plane containing ψ (and negative in most such planes), even though some parallel flows—such as those with convex velocity profiles on short tori—are Eulerian stable.
equivalent_formulation: In the paper’s nearby reformulation, D_μ(M) is not a Riemannian symmetric space because the geodesic central symmetry about the identity in D_μ(M) is not an isometry of the L2 metric.
justification: The draft is already very close to the paper’s actual target. Its central subject, metric, and motivation match Section 5.3 exactly. The only substantive sharpening needed is to align it with the paper’s official wording (‘How far...’), add the paper’s precise notion of failure of symmetry (geodesic central symmetry not being an L2-isometry, as opposed to group inversion), and include the concrete torus-flow paradox and the paper’s resolution via the non-symmetric or ‘chiral’ geometry of D_μ(M).
